questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.**

Are you looking forward ______ Nikhil again?
questions.solution:
​The correct answer is **'****to seeing'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In this case “to” is a **preposition**, and you always need to use the ‘ing’ form **(gerund)** after a **preposition**.
 
• ‘looking forward’ is a** phrasal verb**. A phrasal verb contains a **verb **and a **preposition** and in this case, two prepositions (forward and to).
 
• To look forward to is a** transitive verb** which means that it needs an **object** ( a noun or a verb).
 
• As ‘seeing’ is a **gerund** (noun form of verb), the answer should be 'to seeing'.
 
• This option uses the gerund form "seeing" after the preposition "to." It is the most appropriate choice as it maintains parallel structure and conveys the idea of anticipation or expectation. "Looking forward to seeing" is a common phrase used to express excitement about a future event.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Are you looking forward *to seeing*__ Nikhil again?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **seeing**

 
 
• This option uses the gerund form "seeing" as the object of the verb "looking forward." While gerunds can function as nouns, in this context, it feels incomplete. "Looking forward" is typically followed by a preposition such as "to" to indicate what is being anticipated.
 
 
 
• **to see**
 
 
• This option uses the infinitive form "to see" as the object of the verb "looking forward." The infinitive form is commonly used after "looking forward" to express anticipation or expectation. It is a valid choice and grammatically correct.
 
 
 
• **to be seeing**
 
 
• This option uses the present progressive form "to be seeing" as the object of the verb "looking forward." However, using the present progressive form in this context suggests ongoing or continuous action, which may not be appropriate. "Looking forward" implies anticipation of a specific event or action, rather than an ongoing process.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blank.**

If you ______ your book, I'd like to borrow it now.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **option 4)** i.e. __**have finished.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is a conditional sentence__ having a resultant clause referring to __a future time__.
 
• So the conditional clause must be in__ the present tense__.
 
• As the sentence talks about the completion of the book, we need to use** the perfect tense**.
 
• **Perfect tense**: __Sub+has/have+main verb the main verb+other words.__
 
• So the correct form to be used here is "__**have finished**__**"**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

There are** five main ways of constructing conditional sentences **in English. In all cases, these sentences are made up of an** if clause and a main clause**. In many negative conditional sentences, there is an equivalent sentence construction using "**unless**" instead of "**if**".

 

 
 

 **Conditional sentence type**
 ** Usage **
 ** If clause verb tense**
 ** Main clause verb tense**
 
 
 
 

 **Zero**
 General truths
 Simple present
 Simple present
 
 

 **Type 1**
 A possible condition and its probable result
 Simple present
 Simple future
 
 

 **Type 2**
 A hypothetical condition and its probable result
 Simple past
 Present conditional or**
 Present continuous conditional
 
 

 **Type 3**
 An unreal past condition and its probable result in the past
 Past perfect
 Perfect conditional
 
 

 **Mixed type**
 An unreal past condition and its probable result in the present
 Past perfect
 Present conditional
 
 

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/51867102c7c2f369f6e29d2efe025e3b3367c68261ec20262828d84ca5c8f854.png] **__Hinglish__**

__
 
• दिया गया वाक्य एक सशर्त वाक्य (conditional sentence) है__ जिसका परिणामी खंड __भविष्य के समय का__ संदर्भ देता है।
 
• तो सशर्त खंड (conditional clause) __वर्तमान काल__ में होना चाहिए।
 
• जैसा कि वाक्य पुस्तक के पूरा होने की बात करता है, हमें पूर्ण काल (perfect tense) का उपयोग करने की आवश्यकता है ।
 
• पूर्ण काल : __Sub+has/have+main verb the main verb+other words.__
 
• तो यहां इस्तेमाल किया जाने वाला सही फॉर्म "have finished" है ।

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

His first movement after the shock ________ to work in his loom; and he went on with this unremittingly.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **option 3**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• This is a compound sentence and there are two verbs in this sentence named **'had been'(BE**) and **'went'.**
 
• "he **went **on with this unremittingly" in this part of the sentence we find '**went' **is the past indefinite form of verb **'Go**'. So the tense of the entire sentence is in past. 
 
• Two verbs with their past indefinite form **can not co-exist together **in a same sentence. Because two facts can not happen at the same time. For example-
 
 
• The patient **had died **before the doctor** came.**
 
• The school prayer **had started** before I** reached.**
 
 
 
• So while there are two main verbs present in a sentence in **past tense**, one of the verbs must be placed in its **past participle form (V3)** in order to justify its action earlier than the other verb present there.
 
• Two main verbs in this sentence are '**be'** and '**go'.** Since '**went' **is in past indefinite form , **'be'** verb should be placed in its** past participle** form . So the correct answer is '**had been'.​**

​Therefore, the correct statement is **His first movement after the shock had been to work in his loom; and he went on with this unremittingly. **

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• The 1st option is **incorrect** as '**was been**' is the past indefinite form of verb '**be' **and it is in **passive voice.** That doesn't signify the meaning of the sentence.
 
• The 2nd option is** incorrect **as '**has being**' is an incorrect structure of tense. As** V3** is to be placed after **have/has/had,** but here being is a** V4 **form of '**be**' verb. Moreover '**has' **is present form so it doesn't go with another verb which is in** past** in the same sentence. 
 
• Option 4 is **incorrect** as **'have been'** is signifies** present** tense of the **action/verb**. So it can not be used having another verb in **past tense** in the same sentence.

questions.question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

The victim was ______ in the back of his head.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Shot**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word "**shot**" is the correct choice to fill in the blank in the sentence.
 
• "shot" - This is the past participle form of the verb "shoot."
 
• In this context, it is used to describe an action that has already happened, indicating that the victim was indeed shot in the back of his head.
 
• When describing actions that occurred in the past, it's common to use the past participle form of the verb, which is "shot."
 
• So, the most appropriate option is "**shot**" because it correctly conveys the past action of someone being shot in the back of their head.

Hence, **option 1** is the correct answer.

**Complete sentence**: *The victim was shot __in the back of his head.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• "**Shooting**" is the present participle form of the verb "shoot." It indicates an ongoing action, which is not suitable for this sentence because it describes a completed action.
 
• "**Shoot**" is the base form of the verb and does not fit in this context as it doesn't convey the past tense required for the sentence.
 
• "**Shooted**" is not a correct word in standard English. The past tense of "shoot" is "shot," not "shooted."

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

In the morning we were up at ____ of day, and down to the nigger cabins to pet the dogs.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**break**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The phrase "**break of day**" is an idiomatic expression that means early morning or dawn. It is the most appropriate expression to fit in the blank.
 
• The other options: "**breach**," "**brake**," and "**breech**" do not fit the context.
 
• A "**breach**" refers to breaking a rule or agreement, a "**brake**" is a device for stopping a vehicle, and "**breech**" generally refers to the back part of a gun barrel or the buttocks of a human body.

​Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 1**'.

**Complete Sentence:** In the morning we were up at break of day, and down to the nigger cabins to pet the dogs.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.**

______ many cooks spoil the broth.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Too.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**​​

__
 
• ​Let's look at the proverb given below:
 
 
• **too many cooks spoil the broth- **if too many people are involved in a task or activity, it will not be done well.
 
 
 
• Example:
 
 
• *I sincerely hope that you have taken care that **too many cooks will not spoil the broth** in this event.*
 
 
 
• ​**Idioms **and **proverbs/sayings** are always used in their **original form** i.e. without any change. Hence 'too' will be the correct choice here.

* *​​​​ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__​**

 
• ​​Let's look at the difference between the following adjectives:
 
 
• few- hardly any. (used in a negative sense)
 
• a few- some but not many.
 
• the few- not many but all that is available.
 
• **so** - very, extremely, or to such a degree
 
 
 
• The words "so" and "too" are both adverbs that indicate a degree or extent, but they are used differently in sentences.
 
• **Use of "So"**
 
 
• "So" is used to indicate a degree or extent of a particular quality, often followed by an adjective or adverb, and it usually precedes a result or consequence introduced by "that."
 
• **Example : **"The movie was so interesting that we decided to watch it again."
 
• In this example, "so" is used to describe the extent of the movie being interesting, leading to the result of deciding to watch it again.
 
 
 
• **Use of "Too"**
 
 
• "Too" is used to indicate that there is more of a particular quality than is desired, needed, or suitable. It conveys the idea of excess and is often followed by an adjective or adverb.
 
• **Example :** "The soup is too hot to eat right now."
 
• In this example, "too" is used to describe the soup as having an excess amount of heat, implying that it is not suitable for eating immediately.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.**

Please sign these documents ______ ink so that they can be preserved.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** option 4) i.e. 'in'.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__****

__
 
• We always use the preposition 'in'__ when we describe some characteristic intrinsic to the writing itself.
 
• IN: To write in something (where 'in' denotes a method or style, not location or position) is to describe some characteristic intrinsic to the writing itself:
 __
 
• in cursive
 
• in Russian
 
• in Ink
 
 
 
• **The correct sentence:** "*Please sign these documents** in** ink so that they can be preserved.*"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/9074044cf96dc1d09ca89eac99180c3d7440ade1b364d09d47931959bf693cc8.png] **Confusion Points__**

__
 
• You might get confused with in and with. But, there is a difference:
 
• WITH: To write with something (where 'with' indicates agency and not accompaniment) usually relates something about the writer, the writer's tools, or the writing process; I can write
 
 
• with a feather quill
 
• with a flourish
 
• with the memory still fresh in my mind
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Prepositions show the relationship between 2 words :

 
• **With-**- is used for instruments: "*She hit him with a stick.*"
 
• **By**-- is used for agents: "*It was written by a great poet."*
 
• **From**-- is used to show the starting point: "*The concert is from 6 p.m. onwards.*"

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate words to fill in the blank.**

The job offer was too good for Ranjith to ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**turn down**"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given words are examples of **phrasal verbs.**
 
• The meaning of a phrasal verb is different from the meaning of its parts.
 
• Let's look at the meaning of given phrasal verbs.
 
 
• **Turn back:** go back in the direction from which one has come.
 
• **Turn off: **stop the operation or flow of something by means of a tap, switch, or button; leave one road in order to join another.
 
• **Turn down**: reject something offered or proposed.
 
• **Turn out: **to develop in a particular way, or to have a particular result.
 
 
 
• The given sentence conveys the meaning that the job offer was too good to be rejected.
 
• As per the meaning of given phrasal verbs, **"turn down"** is the most appropriate answer to fill the blank.
 
 
• **Example**: *She refused my request to **turn down**__ the volume of the radio.*
 
 
 
• Hence, the correct answer is** option 3**.

Let's see the meaning of the given words-

questions.question:
**Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.**

We won an unprecedented pardon from ______ -President Karzai, and Gulnaz was freed.
questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is **Then.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The correct answer to fill in the blank is** "then."**
 
• The word 'won' should indicate the granting of pardon from the president of the past time.
 
• **Then** means **(at) that time (in the past or in the future)**.
 
 
• Example: I wanted to live in the city, but my **then husband **(= the man who was my husband at that time) preferred the country.
 
 
 
• So "then-President Karzai" means that at the time when this event happened, Karzai was the president. 
 
• Thus, the correct answer is **Option 1.**

**Correct Sentence**__: *We won an unprecedented pardon from __**then**__-President Karzai, and Gulnaz was freed.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• The other options do not fit grammatically or contextually:
 
• "**Those**" is a pronoun that refers to a specific group of people or things. 
 
• **"At time"** is a phrase that does not provide a clear sense of time or indicate a specific point in time. It lacks the specificity required in this sentence.
 
• **"Later"** is an adverb that indicates a subsequent time or a point in the future.
